title: How NVIDIA Mission Control 2.5 Brings Autonomous Recovery to Kubernetes | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA Mission Control 2.5 extends its autonomous recovery engine, previously limited to Slurm HPC workloads, to Kubernetes workloads managed by NVIDIA Run:ai. The engine splits recovery into a scheduler, a job-recovery service and a hardware-recovery service, with a stated aim of self-healing AI factories and better use of accelerator capacity.

insights.claim: Modern AI factories run distributed training jobs across hundreds of nodes for days or weeks, so hardware anomalies, software errors, network timeouts and resource contention must be handled proactively. Manual intervention, static checkpointing and reactive monitoring do not scale with dozens of concurrent multi-node workloads on shared infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Ryan Prout
insights.so_what: Cluster uptime and automated recovery are becoming product features, not just operations, in AI infrastructure.
insights.quote: Traditional approaches that rely on manual intervention, static checkpointing, and reactive monitoring simply don’t scale

insights.claim: The autonomous recovery engine, which detects, diagnoses and recovers from anomalies across the stack, was previously limited to HPC workloads on Slurm. Mission Control 2.5 now extends it to Kubernetes-based workloads managed with NVIDIA Run:ai.
insights.speaker: Ryan Prout
insights.so_what: Extending to Kubernetes brings the recovery layer to the large share of AI platforms that run on Kubernetes rather than Slurm.

insights.claim: NVIDIA's stated vision is that AI factories should be self-healing systems where failures are detected instantly, recovery decisions reflect workload context and failure type, and jobs resume automatically with minimal wasted compute.
insights.speaker: Ryan Prout
insights.so_what: The aim is autonomous operations, which matters for operating cost as clusters grow.
insights.quote: AI factories should be self-healing systems

insights.claim: The engine has three roles: the scheduler (NVIDIA Run:ai, the default Kubernetes scheduler in Mission Control) places workloads; the autonomous job recovery service classifies failures using failure history and job topology; the autonomous hardware recovery service monitors nodes and GPUs, removes anomalies from scheduling and runs diagnostics.
insights.speaker: Ryan Prout
insights.so_what: Splitting workload context from infrastructure health is the design that makes recovery portable across schedulers.
insights.locator: The three roles in the loop

insights.claim: Keeping responsibilities separate is what makes the model portable: job recovery need not repair hardware, hardware recovery need not understand every training framework, and the scheduler can steer work to ready capacity without waiting for root-cause diagnosis.
insights.speaker: Ryan Prout
insights.so_what: Modularity lets NVIDIA support more schedulers without rebuilding the logic.
insights.quote: Keeping these responsibilities separate is what makes the model portable.

themes.theme: Failure paths: fault, transient error, early degradation

insights.claim: On a hardware fault during training, recovery splits into two parallel tracks. The job service identifies the suspect node and the scheduler restarts or reschedules the job on healthy nodes, while the hardware service isolates the node and runs diagnostics, so the workload does not wait for root-cause analysis.
insights.speaker: Ryan Prout
insights.so_what: Decoupling job restart from diagnosis cuts downtime after a fault.
insights.quote: The workload doesn’t wait for root-cause analysis before recovery begins

insights.claim: For transient software faults the job recovery service uses failure history to retry per scheduler policy instead of quarantining healthy hardware. This avoids operator noise and avoids shrinking the scheduling pool, and repeated failures are still surfaced.
insights.speaker: Ryan Prout
insights.so_what: Restraint avoids pulling healthy GPUs out of the pool, which protects utilization.
insights.quote: The value of this path is restraint.

insights.claim: The hardware recovery service can detect degradation such as repeated GPU health warnings or connectivity problems and remove a node from scheduler eligibility before a job lands on it. The aim is that a known-risk node does not become tomorrow's AI training outage.
insights.speaker: Ryan Prout
insights.so_what: Proactive removal turns outages into maintenance events.
insights.quote: The system reduces the chance that a known-risk node becomes tomorrow’s AI training outage.

insights.claim: NVIDIA says Mission Control 2.5 gives platform teams a consistent recovery model across Kubernetes and Slurm estates, and that for the business the benefit is better utilization of valuable accelerator capacity as systems spend less time stalled.
insights.speaker: Ryan Prout
insights.so_what: The value claim is utilization of expensive GPUs, though the post gives no quantified results.
insights.quote: the benefit is better utilization of valuable accelerator capacity

insights.claim: Mission Control 2.5 is available now. Other highlights are a beta AI-enabled network anomaly detection service, central Keycloak authentication, extra security and Kubernetes hardening, and early access for NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72.
insights.speaker: Ryan Prout
insights.so_what: Early access for Vera Rubin NVL72 indicates the software is being prepared for NVIDIA's next rack-scale generation.
insights.quote: Early access for NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72
